The town had a department for unfinished things.

It occupied two rooms above the public swimming pool, where the air smelled of chlorine and wet wool. There was no sign outside. People found it because someone told them, usually in a lowered voice, as though recommending a discreet dentist. Inside, a woman named Ada sat behind a desk with a green lamp. Behind her stood shelves full of objects that seemed ordinary until you looked closely: a sweater with one sleeve, a letter ending halfway through a sentence, a wooden bird that had never been given wings.

Ada did not finish these things. That was the first misunderstanding she had to correct. People arrived carrying their broken intentions and assumed she would repair them.

“I keep them,” she explained.

“For how long?”

“Until you know.”

Most people disliked this answer. They wanted a date, a fee, a form with numbered boxes. Ada had forms, but they asked unhelpful questions. *What did you believe this would become?* *Who were you when you began?* There was a space at the bottom for anything the applicant preferred not to explain. It was almost always filled.

One November morning, a man brought in a door.

He maneuvered it up the stairs sideways, apologizing whenever it struck the wall. He was perhaps seventy, with a broad, embarrassed face and sawdust caught in the seams of his coat. The door was small, painted yellow, with a round window near the top.

“For a treehouse,” he said.

Ada looked at the door, then at him.

“My daughter’s.”

He rubbed a thumb against a patch of paint. Downstairs, someone blew a whistle. The sound rose through the floorboards, sharp and official.

“She’s forty-three now,” he added.

Ada fetched the large-object form.

The man’s name was Daniel. He had built the platform, he explained, and two of the walls. Then his mother became ill. Then work became uncertain. Then winter came, and the following spring his daughter had discovered other children, other gardens, other ways of spending an afternoon. The platform remained in the tree for years. Eventually the tree grew around one of the bolts.

“I kept meaning to take it down.”

“The platform?”

“The idea.”

Ada nodded. She had a shelf of university applications from people approaching retirement. She understood that structures could remain standing after their practical use had ended.

Daniel left the door and returned the following Thursday.

He said he had been nearby, though Ada knew he lived across town. He looked at the shelves. There were three incomplete jigsaw puzzles, a proposal for a neighborhood orchestra, and a jar containing the first seventeen folded cranes of someone’s intended thousand.

“Do they ever come back for them?” he asked.

“Sometimes.”

“And finish?”

“Sometimes.”

This irritated him.

“You don’t say much.”

“I used to explain more,” Ada said. “People generally remembered the part they needed anyway.”

Daniel considered this, then asked whether she wanted tea.

After that, he came every Thursday. He brought tea in a flask because the department’s kettle tasted faintly of pennies. Ada provided biscuits from a tin whose lid showed a castle neither of them could identify. They rarely discussed the door. Instead they talked about the swimming lessons below, the difficulty of buying good pears, and the strange conviction among younger people that every surface needed a password. Daniel sometimes repaired small things around the office. He tightened a chair leg and unstuck a drawer. Ada allowed this, provided he asked first and did not touch anything on the shelves.

In January, Ada was absent.

A note on the desk said she would return Monday. Daniel stood in the doorway holding the flask. Without her, the room looked less mysterious. The carpet was worn through beside the filing cabinet. A damp patch had spread across the ceiling. He noticed, beneath her desk, a cardboard box he had never seen before.

It held a pair of walking boots, a map, and a photograph of a woman standing beside a mountain.

When Ada returned, he asked about it.

“My sister,” she said.

“Were you going somewhere?”

“We were.”

He waited.

“We postponed.”

That was all she offered, and he did not ask again. But something altered afterward. He had imagined Ada as the keeper of a condition from which she was somehow exempt, like a lifeguard who never entered the water. Now he noticed how carefully she lowered herself into her chair, and how she sometimes paused over the forms before filing them. He began carrying the tea upstairs in two smaller flasks. Neither mentioned it. One Thursday, while Ada searched for a receipt, he looked at the yellow door and realized he could no longer remember his daughter’s childhood height.

In March, he telephoned his daughter.

He asked if she remembered the treehouse. She laughed.

“The squirrel palace?”

“Is that what we called it?”

“That’s what I called it. You were very serious about keeping the squirrels out.”

He had remembered her waiting at the window, disappointed. She remembered stealing screws from his toolbox to use as money in elaborate games. When he apologized, she went quiet.

“Dad,” she said eventually, “I wanted you to come up there with me.”

The following Thursday, Daniel collected the door. Ada helped him down the stairs. Neither of them discussed the form.

He made it into a little cupboard for his granddaughter. The round window showed shelves of crayons, stones, and plastic animals. Its yellow paint clashed magnificently with the kitchen.

In April, Ada took a week off. She did not climb the mountain. She caught a train to the town below it and walked as far as a lake, where she ate a cheese sandwich in the wind.

When she returned, Daniel asked how it had been.

“Cold,” she said.

He poured the tea.

After a while, she took a photograph from her bag and slid it across the desk.
